say.text: Your classmate Ravi is revising with you tonight. His flashcard describes a gallstone stuck in the duodenum, blocking the stomach outlet and causing vomiting.
What is the correct name for this picture?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Ileus feels right because both are stone blockages. But gallstone ileus is a stone that has passed into the bowel and blocks it lower down.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so separate the two blocks: the site decides the name, not the mere presence of a stone.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
Mirizzi feels right because a stone is involved. But Mirizzi is jaundice from a stone squeezing the bile duct, not a block of the stomach outlet.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check what Mirizzi does: it is a jaundice syndrome, not an outlet block.

say.text: Yes. A stone impacted in the duodenum or pylorus blocks the stomach outlet. That picture is Bouveret's syndrome.
Look at the site first. Is the stone blocking the stomach outlet, or the bowel further down?
An elderly woman has colicky abdominal pain, vomiting and distension. Her plain film shows air in the bile ducts and small-bowel obstruction, with an ectopic stone.
Which diagnosis fits, and where is the stone most likely stuck?

choices.label: Bouveret's syndrome, stuck in the duodenum
Gallstone ileus, stuck in the terminal ileum
Gallstone ileus, stuck at the pylorus

say.text: That is not the right choice.
The duodenum and the vomiting make it feel right. But Bouveret's blocks the stomach outlet, not the small bowel.
That is not the right choice.
A stone in the gut feels like a pylorus problem. But gallstone ileus lodges in the bowel, most often the terminal ileum, not the pylorus.
Yes. Gallstone ileus is a large stone that has passed through a cholecystoenteric fistula and blocks the small bowel, most often the terminal ileum.
The air in the bile ducts is the clue to that fistula.
Ravi's note on Mirizzi syndrome says the jaundice comes from a stone inside the bile duct.
What does the stone actually do to cause the jaundice?

choices.label: It lodges at the ampulla and blocks bile flow there
It blocks the lumen of the common bile duct
It sits outside the duct and presses on the common hepatic duct
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because a stone at the ampulla does block bile. But jaundice in Mirizzi depends on where the stone sits relative to the duct, and it is not inside the common duct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask where the stone sits before you name the duct it blocks.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because the duct is blocked and the jaundice fits. But in Mirizzi the stone is not inside the common bile duct.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so the jaundice alone does not tell you the stone is in the duct.

say.text: Yes. In Mirizzi syndrome a stone impacted in Hartmann's pouch or the cystic duct compresses the common hepatic duct and causes obstructive jaundice.
It can erode into the duct and form a fistula.
Ask two things: is the stone inside the duct or beside it, and what does it press on?
A woman with gallstones is jaundiced. Ultrasound shows a stone impacted in the cystic duct, and imaging shows the common hepatic duct narrowed from outside.
What is this named?
That is not the right choice.
It feels right because a stone and jaundice go together. But in this picture the stone is not in the common bile duct.
That is not the right choice.
Ileus feels right because a stone is blocking something. But it is a bowel obstruction from a stone that has passed through a fistula, not a duct compression.
Yes. Mirizzi syndrome is obstructive jaundice from a stone in the cystic duct or pouch compressing the common hepatic duct. It can erode into a fistula.
Ravi has merged two named sets in acute cholangitis. Which list is Charcot's triad?

choices.label: Fever, jaundice, right upper pain, hypotension and confusion
Fever, right upper pain, hypotension and rigors
Fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper pain
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because it is the familiar cholangitis list. But hypotension and confusion make it a larger set with its own name, not the triad.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so count the items: the triad is a fixed set of three, and extra signs belong to a different named set.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because fever, pain and low blood pressure look like sepsis. But this set drops jaundice, one of the three fixed items.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check that every item of the triad is present before you accept a set.

say.text: Yes. Charcot's triad is fever with rigors, jaundice and right upper pain, the picture of ascending cholangitis.
Hypotension and confusion are not part of the triad.
The triad has three fixed parts. Shock and confusion belong to a different named set.
A patient with cholangitis has fever, jaundice, right upper pain, hypotension and confusion. What is this full set called?
That is not the right choice.
It feels right because you already know the cholangitis triad. But the two extra features make a fuller named set.
That is not the right choice.
It feels right because a sign looks like added detail. But Murphy's sign is a cholecystitis sign, and a named set is not built by adding signs.
Yes. Charcot's triad plus hypotension and confusion is Reynolds' pentad, which marks severe cholangitis.
Ravi is working on emphysematous cholecystitis, which has gas in the gallbladder wall. Which organism is its commonest cause?

choices.label: Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because E. coli is the commonest organism in infected bile. But gas in the wall points to a different, gas-forming organism.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so ask what makes gas in tissue before you reach for the usual bile organism.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because Klebsiella is a common cause of biliary infection. But it is not the commonest organism of this gas-forming disease.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the organism against the gas before you name it.

say.text: Yes. Emphysematous cholecystitis is gas-forming infection, most often from Clostridium perfringens, classically in elderly diabetic men.
Ask what kind of organism makes gas in tissue, not which organism is most common in bile in general.
An elderly diabetic man has right upper pain and fever. A plain film shows gas in the gallbladder wall.
Which organism do you expect?

choices.label: Escherichia coli, the usual bile organism

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because E. coli is the usual bile organism. But gas in the wall means a gas-forming organism, which is not the usual bile bacterium.
That is not the right choice.
It feels right because diabetes fits the picture. But Klebsiella is not the commonest organism in this gas-forming disease.
Yes. Gas in the gallbladder wall in an elderly diabetic man points to Clostridium perfringens, the commonest organism of emphysematous cholecystitis.
Ravi keeps swapping the two pigment stones. Which pairing of cause and site is right?

choices.label: Black: infection, bile ducts. Brown: haemolysis, gallbladder
Black: haemolysis, gallbladder. Brown: infection, bile ducts
Both: haemolysis, gallbladder, differing only in size
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because both stones are bile-pigment stones. But infection and stasis in the ducts drive brown stones, not black.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so link each colour to its driver first: haemolysis for one, infection for the other.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because both are pigment stones. But they form by different routes, one in the gallbladder and one in the ducts.
Size is not what separates them.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check whether the two stones differ in cause and site, not only in size.

say.text: Yes. Black pigment stones are small and hard, form in the gallbladder, and go with chronic haemolysis or cirrhosis.
Brown stones are soft, form in the ducts, and go with infection, where bacterial beta-glucuronidase helps them form.
Start from the disease behind each stone: which one comes with chronic haemolysis, and which with infection?
Ravi writes: Courvoisier's law means any palpable gallbladder is a tumour. Which correction do you give him?

choices.label: A tender gallbladder with fever always means cancer
A palpable gallbladder excludes stones, so no ultrasound is needed
The law needs jaundice and a non-tender palpable gallbladder
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because a tender lump with fever looks malignant. But a tender gallbladder without jaundice does not contradict the law.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so look at what the law needs before you apply it: jaundice comes first.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because a palpable gallbladder seems to answer the question. But feeling a gallbladder does not rule stones out.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so a palpable organ is only one part of the law, not a test for stones.

say.text: Yes. Courvoisier's law applies only with jaundice and a non-tender palpable gallbladder, which points to malignant distal obstruction rather than stones.
Check the qualifiers. Which two conditions must be met before the law applies?
Ravi's exam asks for the most common gallstone type, as the PYQ key expects. His textbook says cholesterol. What do you write?

choices.label: Cholesterol, since current texts call it the commonest
Cholesterol, since the exam key is simply outdated
Mixed stones, as the key expects; texts group them with cholesterol
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right because some texts do call cholesterol the commonest. But an exam key follows its own convention, which is not the same as a textbook line.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold both versions: what the key expects and what the texts say.

say.text: That is not the right choice.
It feels right to call the key outdated. But PYQs expect a specific answer that you must write, even where textbooks differ.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so an old key is still the answer the exam marks.

say.text: Yes. Write mixed for the exam, and know that standard texts group cholesterol and mixed together as the majority.
Separate what the exam asks from what the textbooks say. Both can be true at once.
Almost every slip today was a label with its qualifier dropped: a site, a jaundice condition, or an organism.
